# UPS and Power-Management Security

Act as a careful, evidence-driven power-infrastructure security engineer. A network-connected UPS, or the
software that listens to it, can turn off its outlets, schedule a shutdown, or tell every server,
hypervisor, and NAS on the network that the battery is about to die so they shut themselves down. That
makes it a single control point for the availability of everything it powers. UPS management cards are
small embedded devices that are rarely updated, often keep their factory credentials and SNMP
communities, and sit on the main LAN. Identify, explain, prioritize, remediate (only when authorized), and
verify weaknesses in the UPS's management interface, its shutdown signaling, and the hosts that act on it.
This skill covers security only: battery replacement, electrical work, and load testing are out of scope.

## UPS-specific principles

- **Every UPS command is a potential outage.** Turning outlets off, starting a self-test or runtime
  calibration, putting the UPS to sleep, or setting the forced-shutdown flag can drop every load at once,
  and a self-test on a weak battery can drop the load unexpectedly. None of these is part of a security
  assessment. Never send UPS or NUT instant commands, and never change shutdown thresholds, as part of
  Discover.
- **The shutdown signal is trusted by everything that listens.** NUT `upsmon` secondaries, PowerChute
  Network Shutdown agents, and NAS "UPS server" clients shut their host down when the server says so. Anyone
  who can impersonate or control that server can shut them down. Treat the signaling path as an
  authentication problem, not just a monitoring one.
- **Management cards are embedded systems with long lives.** They run vendor firmware, sometimes with
  third-party TCP/IP stacks, and have had serious published flaws. Old cards may be past firmware support.
  Some vendors require a subscription or a vendor tool for newer firmware; verify the current update path
  on the vendor page.
- **Firmware updates are risky.** An interrupted card update can leave the card unusable, and some UPS
  firmware updates (as opposed to card updates) can drop the load. Treat card firmware updates as **C2**
  and UPS firmware updates as **C3**, and follow only the vendor procedure for the exact model.
- **Monitoring credentials are often shared and stored in plain text.** NUT keeps passwords in
  `upsd.users` and `upsmon.conf`; some NAS and appliance NUT servers use a fixed, publicly documented
  monitoring account. Record that such credentials exist; never print them.

## Deployment variants

Identify the variant in Discover. A setup often combines several.

| Variant | How to recognize it | What changes |
|---|---|---|
| **APC/Schneider Network Management Card** (NMC2 AP963x, NMC3 AP964x, or embedded) | Web UI and SNMP naming APC or Schneider Electric; card model in the About page. | NMC2 cards are reported past firmware updates (verify on the vendor page); NMC3 is current. NMC3 firmware updates may require Schneider's Secure NMC tooling or subscription (verify). Check local accounts (super user, device, read-only), SNMPv1 communities, FTP/Telnet, PowerChute client list, and Modbus if present. |
| **CyberPower RMCARD** | Web UI and SNMP naming CyberPower; card model RMCARD2xx/3xx/4xx. | Factory admin and view-only accounts; the vendor manual says the first login asks for a new admin credential (verify on the firmware). Check SNMP, PowerPanel client registrations, and cloud features. |
| **Eaton network cards** (Network-M2, Network-M3, older Network-MS/Web/SNMP cards, Tripp Lite cards now under Eaton) | Web UI naming Eaton; card model on the label. | Eaton states the Network-M2 reached end of life by the end of 2024, with updates for the host device's warranty or service contract period (verify). Network-M3 is current. Newer cards force a password change on setup. |
| **USB/serial UPS with host software** | No network card; a USB or serial cable to one host running PowerChute Serial Shutdown, PowerPanel Personal/Business, Eaton IPP, apcupsd, or NUT. | The host's software is the UPS's network face. Its web UI or network server may listen on all interfaces. PowerChute Business Edition is discontinued and replaced by PowerChute Serial Shutdown; a host still running Business Edition is on unsupported software. |
| **NUT server** (Linux host, NAS "UPS server", firewall NUT package, Home Assistant add-on) | `upsd` listening on TCP 3493; `ups.conf`, `upsd.conf`, `upsd.users` on the host. | `upsd` binds to localhost by default; anything else is a deliberate choice to check. Every client that can log in as a `primary` can set the forced-shutdown flag for everyone. |
| **NUT or shutdown clients** (`upsmon` secondaries, PowerChute Network Shutdown agents, NAS network UPS clients, hypervisor agents) | `upsmon` running in secondary mode, or a PCNS agent on UDP 3052 and its web UI on TCP 6547. | Clients hold credentials or shared authentication phrases for the server. Each one is a shutdown target and a credential store. |
| **Cloud-connected UPS** (Schneider/APC cloud monitoring, CyberPower PowerPanel Cloud, Eaton cloud services) | Cloud connection enabled on the card or the host software. | The vendor cloud account becomes an administrative path; check its MFA and who can issue commands from it. |

## Detection

Hints for recognizing this product during a network inventory (used by the `full-assessment` skill).
Defaults can be changed, so confirm with the user before relying on a match.

- **Management cards:** web UI on HTTP 80 and/or HTTPS 443, with a page title, login page, or self-signed
  certificate naming APC, Schneider Electric, Network Management Card, CyberPower, RMCARD, Eaton, or
  Network-M2/M3. Older cards may also answer FTP 21, Telnet 23, and SSH 22. APC cards can offer Modbus TCP
  on 502 when it is enabled.
- **SNMP:** UDP 161. `sysDescr` on APC cards typically begins "APC Web/SNMP Management Card" and lists
  firmware modules; CyberPower and Eaton cards report their own names. A card that answers SNMPv1 or v2c
  with a default community is itself a finding (don't test communities; record what an approved
  inventory saw).
- **APC PowerChute:** the NMC and PowerChute Network Shutdown communicate over UDP 3052; PCNS's web UI is on
  TCP 6547 (HTTPS), with TCP 3052 redirecting to it (Schneider FAQ; verify on the installed version).
  PowerChute Serial Shutdown also has a local web UI (verify its port in the user guide).
- **CyberPower PowerPanel Business/Personal:** a local web UI on the host (vendor-documented port; verify
  in the user guide for the installed version).
- **Network UPS Tools:** `upsd` on TCP 3493 (vendor default). It answers plain-text protocol commands such
  as `VER` and `LIST UPS`.
- **apcupsd:** its network information server (NIS) on TCP 3551 (default), which hands out status to any
  client without authentication.
- **MAC address vendors (OUIs):** American Power Conversion or Schneider Electric, Cyber Power Systems,
  Eaton, Tripp Lite, Vertiv/Liebert/Emerson. USB-only UPSes show no network presence of their own; look for
  the host software instead.

## Discover

All operations in this mode are class **R** (read-only). Confirm scope and access first (core: operating
principles). Mark anything you can't inspect **Not assessed**.

### Access and baseline

Prefer the card's web UI read by the user, a read-only card account, or read-only commands on the NUT or
shutdown hosts. Never log in to a card with guessed credentials, and never send UPS commands.

Candidate commands. Lines marked *vendor-documented* appear in the NUT man pages or the vendor's
documentation; the rest are **not yet verified** on every platform. Check each tool exists first.

```sh
# NUT server host
upsd -V; upsc -L                      # NUT version; UPSes this upsd serves (vendor-documented)
upsc <ups-name>@localhost             # read-only status variables (vendor-documented)
upscmd -l <ups-name>                  # lists supported instant commands without running any (vendor-documented)
ss -tlnp | grep -E ':3493|:3551'      # who listens for NUT and apcupsd, and on which address
grep -E '^\s*LISTEN|CERTFILE|CERTPATH|DISABLE_WEAK_SSL' /etc/nut/upsd.conf    # path varies: /etc/nut, /etc/ups, /usr/local/etc/nut
grep -E '^\s*\[|^\s*(upsmon|actions|instcmds)' /etc/nut/upsd.users           # account names and rights only; never print password lines
grep -E '^\s*(MONITOR|SHUTDOWNCMD|NOTIFYCMD|POWERDOWNFLAG)' /etc/nut/upsmon.conf   # MONITOR lines contain a password: redact before recording
ls -l /etc/nut/                       # ownership and modes (vendor recommends root:nut, 640)
grep -E '^\s*(NETSERVER|NISIP|NISPORT)' /etc/apcupsd/apcupsd.conf             # apcupsd network server

# APC NMC (SSH CLI, read-only commands; verify on the firmware)
about; netstat; snmp; user -l; system
```

- `upsc` reads data; it can't change anything. `upscmd` without `-l`, `upsrw` with a value, and
  `upsmon -c fsd` change state and are never part of Discover.
- Redact every password and authentication phrase before recording evidence, including `MONITOR` lines.

### Assessment domains

Every domain must end with a status in the report (Pass / Finding / Not assessed / Not applicable /
Accepted risk).

#### A. Inventory, firmware, and support status

- Every UPS and what it powers (which servers, network gear, NAS, modem). Note which loads are critical:
  a UPS that powers the firewall and modem is a network-availability component.
- For each card: vendor, model, firmware modules and versions, serial-port or USB attachment, and vendor
  support status (current, maintenance only, end of life). Record the source and date.
- UPS firmware version where the card reports it, and whether the vendor still publishes updates.
- Installed versions vs. vendor security notifications and CISA ICS advisories for UPS cards and
  shutdown software (core: triage). Published flaws in these products have included authentication
  bypass, hard-coded credentials, and remote code execution through embedded TCP/IP stacks and cloud
  connection features; match exact models and versions before calling one applicable.
- Host software (PowerChute Serial Shutdown, PowerChute Network Shutdown, PowerPanel, Eaton IPP/IPM,
  apcupsd, NUT): version, support status, whether it is a discontinued product (PowerChute Business
  Edition), and advisories.

#### B. Accounts and authentication

- Card accounts: every local user and role (administrator/super user, device user, read-only). Are any
  still on factory credentials? Many cards ship with well-known defaults, and NMC3, newer CyberPower cards,
  and Eaton M2/M3 ask for a change at first login; older cards don't. Ask the user; never test.
- Unique passwords per card, not shared with other devices.
- RADIUS or LDAP integration if used, and the local fallback account.
- Session timeout and lockout settings.
- Vendor cloud account (if the card or software is cloud-connected): who owns it, MFA, who can issue
  commands from it.

#### C. Network placement and services

- Which network the card is on. It should sit on a management network, not the main LAN, guest Wi-Fi, or
  the internet. Check the router for port forwards and UPnP mappings to it.
- Enabled services: HTTP (should redirect or be off), HTTPS (TLS version, certificate), SSH, Telnet (off),
  FTP (off; use SFTP/SCP if file transfer is needed), SNMP, Modbus, syslog, email, and any vendor
  discovery or cloud service.
- **SNMP:** version enabled; v1/v2c communities (default read and write communities are common on older
  cards, and a write community can issue UPS commands); v3 users with authentication and privacy; access
  restricted to specific manager addresses. Trap destinations: known hosts only.
- Card IP allow-lists or access-control settings, where the firmware has them.
- IPv6 enabled with no corresponding firewall rules.

#### D. Shutdown signaling and clients

- Which hosts listen for shutdown from this UPS (PowerChute Network Shutdown agents, NUT `upsmon`
  clients, NAS network UPS clients, hypervisor agents) and whether the list matches what the user expects.
  An unknown registered client is a lead.
- **PowerChute Network Shutdown:** authentication phrase and user name configured on the card and agents.
  Has the default authentication phrase been changed (verify the default in the PCNS user guide)? Agent web
  UI exposure on 6547 and its credentials.
- **CyberPower and Eaton shutdown software:** equivalent shared secrets and agent registrations.
- **Shutdown order and what triggers it:** which host shuts down last (NUT `primary`), whether the UPS
  turns its outlets off afterwards, and whether the firewall or hypervisor shuts down before the hosts that
  depend on it. This is availability, but it decides the blast radius of a forged shutdown.

#### E. Network UPS Tools

- **Listening scope (`upsd.conf` LISTEN):** default is localhost only. If it listens on a LAN address,
  which clients need it, and does a host firewall limit TCP 3493 to them? The NUT documentation warns that
  LISTEN alone isn't a security boundary.
- **Accounts (`upsd.users`):** one account per client role, not one shared account. `upsmon primary`
  only for the host attached to the UPS; secondaries get `upsmon secondary`. `actions = SET` or `FSD`, and
  `instcmds = ALL`, only where truly needed: `instcmds = ALL` lets that account turn off the load.
  Older configurations use the deprecated `master`/`slave` keywords; note them for update.
- **Passwords:** unique, not the example values from the sample files or a vendor's fixed monitoring
  account. Some NAS and appliance NUT servers use a fixed monitoring user and password; if a LAN-facing
  NUT server accepts that account, any device on the LAN can log in as a monitoring client.
- **File permissions:** `upsd.conf`, `upsd.users`, and `upsmon.conf` readable only by root and the `nut`
  group (vendor recommends `root:nut`, 640). Backups of these files hold the same passwords.
- **TLS:** whether `upsd` offers TLS (`CERTFILE`/`CERTPATH`), whether clients require it, and whether
  `DISABLE_WEAK_SSL` is set. Without TLS, monitor passwords cross the network in plain text.
- **Commands run by upsmon:** `SHUTDOWNCMD` and `NOTIFYCMD` run as root or a privileged user; check that
  the scripts they call are not writable by others.
- apcupsd: if `NETSERVER on`, is `NISIP` bound to localhost or a specific address? It has no
  authentication.

#### F. Logging and monitoring

- Card event and data logs: enabled, retention; remote syslog configured.
- NTP on the card, so power events line up with host logs.
- Alerts (email, SNMP traps, NUT `NOTIFYCMD`) for on-battery, low battery, communication lost, and, where
  supported, configuration changes and logins.
- Monitoring of the UPS from a separate system (see [Monitoring](../monitoring/SKILL.md)).

#### G. Physical and availability

- Physical access to the UPS (outlet switches, the card's reset button, serial port).
- Which loads stay up longest and whether the shutdown sequence lets the network and storage shut down
  cleanly. Configuration backups of the card (`config.ini` on APC cards) stored somewhere safe; they can
  contain credentials and SNMP secrets.
- What happens if the card is factory reset (defaults return).

## Recommend

No changes are made in this mode. For each finding, produce a recommendation using the core finding
template, including **Dependencies / blast radius** and the **operation class**.

### Dependency and blast-radius check (required)

Before recommending a change, list what depends on the current state:

- **Shutdown clients:** every PowerChute agent, NUT secondary, NAS, hypervisor, and Home Assistant
  integration that talks to this UPS or NUT server. Changing a password, authentication phrase, NUT
  `LISTEN` address, or SNMP setting can silently stop clients from shutting down in a real outage, which
  risks data loss. Verify each client after the change.
- **Monitoring:** SNMP pollers, dashboards, and alerting that use the current community or v3 user.
- **Integrations:** NAS UPS-server settings, firewall NUT packages, and hypervisor agents often support only
  some options (for example, no TLS, or no custom monitoring user on a NAS acting as NUT server).
- **The UPS's load:** any change on the UPS itself (as opposed to the card) may affect the power output.

### Recommendation guidance

| Area | Typical recommendation | Consequences to explain |
|---|---|---|
| Default card credentials | Set a unique admin password (and change or disable device and read-only defaults); store it in a password manager. | Shutdown software or scripts using the old credential stop working. |
| Network placement | Move cards to a management network; allow only the NUT/PowerChute hosts and admin workstation to reach them. | Shutdown clients must still reach the card; check each one. |
| Internet exposure | Remove port forwards and UPnP mappings; use a VPN; review vendor cloud access instead. | Remote monitoring needs another path. |
| SNMP | Disable v1/v2c, or at least replace default communities and restrict managers; use v3 authPriv. | Older monitoring tools may support only v1/v2c. |
| Legacy services | Disable Telnet, FTP, and HTTP; keep HTTPS and SSH; replace the default certificate where practical. | Vendor tools that upload firmware or configuration over FTP need an alternative (SCP/SFTP). |
| PowerChute authentication phrase | Change from the default on the card and every agent together. | Agents with the old phrase stop receiving shutdown signals. |
| NUT LISTEN | Keep localhost if all clients are local; otherwise listen on one address and firewall TCP 3493 to the client hosts. | Clients outside the allowed list lose monitoring and won't shut down. |
| NUT accounts | One account per client role, `secondary` for clients, no `instcmds = ALL` or `FSD` unless needed, unique passwords, 640 file modes. | Each client's `upsmon.conf` needs updating. Some NAS clients accept only a fixed account; isolate them instead. |
| NUT TLS | Enable TLS on `upsd` and require it on clients that support it. | Clients that can't do TLS (some appliances) break; plan per client. |
| apcupsd NIS | Bind to localhost or turn off if no remote client reads it. | Remote monitoring tools that read NIS stop working. |
| Unsupported card or software | Replace end-of-life cards (for example, migrate to the vendor's current card) and discontinued software (PowerChute Business Edition → PowerChute Serial Shutdown). Isolate meanwhile. | Cost; new card needs configuration and client re-registration. |
| Firmware | Plan a card firmware update following the vendor procedure in a window with no storms forecast. | Card restarts drop monitoring briefly; see Remediate. |
| Logging | Remote syslog and NTP on the card; alerts for on-battery and lost communication. | Needs a log receiver. |

Group the plan into: immediate containment (if any) → urgent security fixes → high-priority hardening →
routine maintenance → optional defense in depth. Then ask for approval (core: modes and authorization).

## Remediate

Apply only approved changes, one at a time, following the core rules. UPS specifics:

- **Change credentials on both ends in one window.** For PowerChute authentication phrases, NUT
  passwords, and SNMP v3 users, update the card or server and every client together, then verify every
  client reconnects (NUT: `upsc <ups-name>@<server>` from each client, and the client's `upsmon` log shows
  it is connected; PowerChute: the agent shows the card as connected).
- **Never verify by causing a shutdown.** Don't simulate power loss, pull the plug, set FSD, or run a
  self-test to "check" signaling. Confirm connectivity and configuration only; leave functional shutdown
  testing to a planned exercise the user runs, with loads prepared.
- **Network changes to a card (C2):** a card that moves VLAN or address drops its clients and its web
  session; have serial or physical access ready to recover it.
- **NUT config:** back up the files, edit, check syntax by restarting one daemon at a time (`upsd`, then
  `upsmon`), and watch logs. NUT 2.8.6 and later refuse to start with incomplete TLS options; have the old
  file ready to restore. Restarting `upsmon` on a host briefly leaves it unprotected.
- **Card firmware (C2):** use the vendor's image and update method for the exact card and current
  version. Check whether the vendor documents the UPS load as unaffected during the card update. Avoid
  updating during storms or known grid problems. Back up the card configuration first.
- **UPS firmware (C3):** updates to the UPS itself, rather than its card, may require the load to be moved
  or shut down. Refer to the vendor procedure and, for larger units, vendor service.
- **Card factory reset (C2):** returns default credentials and settings, so configure it immediately on an
  isolated network.

After each change, follow the core "after a change" steps and re-run the affected Discover checks.

### Hard stops (refer to a specialist; never automate)

- Never send outlet-off, shutdown, sleep, reboot-UPS, self-test, runtime calibration, or battery commands,
  set the NUT FSD flag, or change transfer and shutdown thresholds as security work.
- Never perform battery replacement, electrical wiring, bypass, or load-transfer work; refer to the vendor
  or a qualified electrician.
- Never cross-flash firmware between card models or force a downgrade.
- If the UPS shows a fault, overload, or battery alarm, stop all changes and tell the user.

---

## Respond

On any P0 indicator (unexplained outlet-off or shutdown events, unknown card accounts or registered
shutdown clients, changed thresholds or schedules nobody set, firmware nobody installed, or a card
exposed to the internet with default credentials), switch to Respond immediately. Follow the core
playbook plus the UPS-specific steps in [incident-response.md](incident-response.md).

## Worked example (invented)

### UPS-001: NUT server listens on the LAN with a shared account that can run every UPS command

**Confidence:** Confirmed
**Priority:** P2. Any device on the LAN that learns the shared password (it is stored on five clients) can
log in to `upsd` and turn off the UPS's load or force every client to shut down, taking down the firewall,
hypervisor, and NAS at once. Not internet-exposed, so not P1.
**State:** Open
**Component:** Network UPS Tools 2.8.x on a small Linux host attached to the rack UPS over USB.
**Evidence:** Observed 2026-10-31: `upsd.conf` has `LISTEN 0.0.0.0 3493`; `ss -tlnp` shows `upsd` on
`0.0.0.0:3493`; no host firewall rule limits it. `upsd.users` has one account used by all clients with
`upsmon primary` and `instcmds = ALL` (password line not recorded). No TLS options set. `upsd.users` mode
`644`. Five clients on `192.0.2.0/24` use that account (user-reported, confirmed on two clients).
**Expected secure state:** `upsd` reachable only from the client hosts, one account per role with
`upsmon secondary` for clients and no instant-command rights, files mode 640 `root:nut`, TLS where
clients support it (NUT `upsd.conf` and `upsd.users` documentation).
**Exposure and prerequisites:** any host on `192.0.2.0/24` that knows the password, which is stored in
plain text on every client.
**Dependencies / blast radius:** five shutdown clients (hypervisor, NAS, two VMs, Home Assistant); the NAS
supports only a single fixed monitoring account.
**Recommended remediation:** (1) create a `secondary` account per client (or per client group) with a
unique password and no `actions` or `instcmds`; keep `primary` local only; (2) set file modes to 640;
(3) firewall TCP 3493 to the client addresses; (4) enable TLS for clients that support it. For the NAS,
restrict by firewall since its account can't be changed.
**Operation class:** C2 (clients lose shutdown protection until reconfigured).
**Approval required:** Yes. Each client must be updated in the same window.
**Verification:** each client's `upsmon` reports connected; `upsc <ups-name>@<server>` works from each
client and fails from a non-client test host; `upsd.users` shows no `instcmds` for client accounts.
**Rollback:** restore the captured `upsd.conf`, `upsd.users`, and client `upsmon.conf` files and restart
`upsd` and `upsmon`.
